entry.sum: An equation $A = B$ states that the expressions $A$ and $B$ have the same value; it is true or false, and it reads the same in both directions, so $7 = 5 + 2$ is as good as $5 + 2 = 7$. An unknown in an equation stands for a number, and a solution is a number that makes the equation true. Equality obeys a few laws (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, substitution), and from them comes the rule that doing the same to both sides keeps an equation's solutions.
key: a = b \implies a + c = b + c
entry.why: Every equation in algebra, and every chain of equal signs in a calculation or proof, relies on reading $=$ as "has the same value as" rather than "write the answer".

links.note: equality, with its reflexive, symmetric and transitive laws and substitution of equals, is part of first-order logic

blocks.body:
An equation such as $3 + 4 = 7$ is a statement: it says that the expression on the left and the expression on the right are two names for one number. Like any statement it is true or false, and it reads equally well backwards: $7 = 3 + 4$ says exactly the same thing.

This reading is what algebra is built on. Solving an equation, rewriting an expression and every chain of equal signs in a calculation depend on it. The commonest early misunderstanding, that $=$ means "now write the answer", works for $3 + 4 = 7$ but fails as soon as an equation looks different.

blocks.title: What an equation says
blocks.body: Arithmetic builds expressions out of numbers and operation signs, and each expression has a value: the number obtained by carrying out its operations. Different expressions can have the same value. The expressions $3 + 4$, $10 - 3$, $5 + 2$ and $7$ itself all have the value 7.

blocks.title: Expression, equation, true and false
blocks.body:
An expression is a number, or numbers combined by operations such as $+$ and $-$: $7$, $3 + 4$ and $10 - 3$ are expressions. An expression names a number; it asserts nothing, so it is neither true nor false.

An equation is two expressions joined by the equal sign $=$, such as $3 + 4 = 10 - 3$. It asserts that the two expressions have the same value. It is true if they do and false if they do not. The sign $\neq$ says that two values differ: $4 + 1 \neq 5 + 2$, since the left side is 5 and the right side is 7.

The sign $=$ is read "equals", "is equal to" or "is the same as". Nothing in the definition says which side holds the calculation and which the result: either side, both or neither may contain operations.

blocks.solution:
Find the value of each side and compare.

(a) $8 - 1 = 7$, so both sides are 7: true. Writing the result first changes nothing.

(b) Both sides are 6: true. An equation need not contain an operation at all.

(c) Both sides are 7: true. Since $a + b = b + a$ for all numbers ([[properties-of-operations]]), this one can be decided without adding.

(d) The sides are 5 and 7: false, and one writes $4 + 1 \neq 5 + 2$.

blocks.title: The equal sign is not a "write the answer" signal
blocks.body:
A very common reading of $=$ is an instruction: do the calculation on the left, then write its result on the right. It gets $3 + 4 = 7$ right, but it rejects $7 = 3 + 4$ as backwards and $6 = 6$ as pointless. Faced with $8 + 4 = \square + 5$ it produces the two typical wrong answers: 12 (the result of the left side, written in the next space) and 17 (all the numbers added up). The correct answer is 7: then the right side is $7 + 5 = 12$ as well, and the two sides balance, as in the figure.

This reading is linked to weaker performance in later algebra, where equations such as $2x + 3 = x + 10$ have work to do on both sides.

blocks.title: A chain of equal signs is only as good as its weakest link
blocks.body: Because each $=$ asserts "same value", a chain $A = B = C = D$ asserts that all four expressions have one value, and then $A = D$ follows (the transitive law, below). That conclusion needs every link to be true. Working out $8 + 4$ and then adding 5, it is tempting to write $8 + 4 = 12 + 5 = 17$. Read as mathematics, the first link claims $8 + 4 = 12 + 5$, which is false (12 against 17). Correct versions are two separate equations, $8 + 4 = 12$ and $12 + 5 = 17$, or a chain in which every link holds: $8 + 4 + 5 = 12 + 5 = 17$.

blocks.title: Compensation
blocks.body:
For whole numbers $a$, $b$ and $k$, whenever the subtractions are possible,

$$(a + k) + (b - k) = a + b \quad\text{and}\quad (a + k) - (b + k) = a - b:$$

moving $k$ from one term of a sum to the other, or shifting both terms of a difference by $k$, leaves the value unchanged.

Sum: $a + b = a + (b - k) + k$, and reordering ([[properties-of-operations]]) gives $(a + k) + (b - k)$. Difference: $a - b$ is the number $d$ with $b + d = a$; then $(b + k) + d = a + k$, so $d = (a + k) - (b + k)$. On a number line $a - b$ is the distance from $b$ to $a$, and moving both points $k$ to the right does not change it.

blocks.body: Decide without adding or subtracting: (a) $52 - 27 = 55 - 30$; (b) $38 + 17 = 40 + 16$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Both terms rise by 3, so the difference is unchanged: true. The right side is the easy one, $55 - 30 = 25$, so this is also a good way to compute $52 - 27$.

(b) 38 rises by 2 but 17 falls by only 1, so the right side is 1 larger: false. Indeed $38 + 17 = 55$ and $40 + 16 = 56$.

items.a: No. It is an expression: it names the number 7 but asserts nothing, so it is neither true nor false.

items.q: Is $9 = 9 + 0$ an equation? Is it true?
items.a: It is an equation (an expression on each side of $=$), and it is true: both sides are 9.

items.hint: Find the value of each side.
items.solution: (a) True: both sides are 6. (b) False: $3 + 4 = 7 \neq 8$. (c) False: the sides are 12 and 10.

items.q: In $4 + 1 = 5 + 2$, change exactly one number to make the equation true. Find every way of doing this.
items.hint: The sides are 5 and 7. Each of the four numbers can be changed.
items.solution: Raise the left side to 7 or lower the right side to 5. Changing the 4 to 6 or the 1 to 3 gives a left side of 7; changing the 5 to 3 or the 2 to 0 gives a right side of 5. So there are exactly four ways: $6 + 1 = 5 + 2$, $4 + 3 = 5 + 2$, $4 + 1 = 3 + 2$, $4 + 1 = 5 + 0$. Each position allows only one new value, because the side it is on must reach one particular total.

items.q: Someone objects that $7 = 3 + 4$ is written backwards and that $6 = 6$ says nothing. Using the definition, explain why both are true equations, and why $A = B$ and $B = A$ always say the same thing.
items.hint: What does an equation assert? Does that assertion mention a left side or a right side?
items.solution: An equation asserts only that its two sides have the same value. In $7 = 3 + 4$ both sides have the value 7, and in $6 = 6$ both have the value 6, so both are true; the definition does not ask for an operation on the left or a single number on the right. "$A$ and $B$ have the same value" and "$B$ and $A$ have the same value" are one statement, so $A = B$ and $B = A$ are true or false together. Nor is $6 = 6$ empty: it is an instance of the reflexive law $a = a$, the starting point of the proofs in the last section.

items.q: A sum is unchanged when one term goes up by $k$ and the other goes down by $k$. Is a difference unchanged when the first term goes up by $k$ and the second goes down by $k$? If not, find the correct rule.
items.solution: No. $10 - 4 = 6$ but $11 - 3 = 8$. In general $(a + k) - (b - k) = a - b + 2k$: raising $a$ adds $k$ to the difference and lowering $b$ adds another $k$. A difference keeps its value when both terms move the same way by the same amount.

blocks.title: Unknowns and solutions
blocks.body: An equation may contain a number that is not known yet: $8 + \square = 11$, $7 = ? - 9$, $x + 3 = 8$. Such an equation is not yet true or false. It becomes one or the other when a number is put in place of the unknown, and the question is which numbers make it true.

blocks.title: Unknown and solution
blocks.body:
An unknown is a symbol in an equation that stands for a number. A solution is a number that makes the equation true when it replaces the unknown; to solve the equation is to find all its solutions. A box, a question mark, a blank or a letter may mark an unknown; the choice of mark changes nothing. Where the same symbol appears twice, it stands for the same number both times.

The solution of $8 + \square = 11$ is 3, because $8 + 3 = 11$ is true and no other number works. Substituting a proposed solution is always a complete check: it leaves an equation with no unknown, which is simply true or false.

blocks.title: One unknown among three numbers
blocks.body:
For whole numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$,

$$a + b = c \iff c - a = b \iff c - b = a,$$

where a statement such as $c - a = b$ includes the claim that the subtraction is possible. (The sign $\iff$ means that each statement implies the other.) So an addition or subtraction equation relating three numbers, one of them unknown, is solved as follows.

- Unknown total, $a + b = \square$: the box is $a + b$.
- Unknown term of a sum, $a + \square = c$: the box is $c - a$.
- Unknown starting number, $\square - b = a$: the box is $a + b$.
- Unknown amount taken away, $c - \square = a$: the box is $c - a$.

There is never more than one solution, and among whole numbers there is one exactly when the subtraction it calls for is possible.

First, uniqueness. If $b < b'$, then $a + b < a + b'$, because adding a larger number gives a larger sum; so at most one whole number $b$ satisfies $a + b = c$. If $a \le c$ there is one, the number of steps in counting on from $a$ to $c$; if $a > c$ there is none, since $a + b \ge a$. Subtraction is defined from this: $c - a$ is that unique number ([[addition-subtraction]]).

So $a + b = c$ holds exactly when $c - a$ exists and equals $b$, which is the first equivalence; since $a + b = b + a$, exchanging $a$ and $b$ gives the second. Each of the four forms in the list is one of these three statements with the unknown in some position, so each has at most one solution.

blocks.solution:
(a) Read it as $\square - 3 = 5$: 3 was taken away and 5 is left, so the starting number is $5 + 3 = 8$. Check: $8 - 3 = 5$.

(b) In the same way the unknown is $7 + 9 = 16$. Check: $16 - 9 = 7$. Here the answer is larger than every number shown, which is exactly what "write the answer" reasoning fails to expect.

(c) The amount taken away is $12 - 9 = 3$. Check: $12 - 3 = 9$.

(d) The box would have to be $4 - 9$, which is not a whole number: $9 + \square$ is at least 9 for every whole number, so it is never 4. The equation has no whole-number solution. Among the integers, which include negative numbers, it has the solution $-5$.

blocks.body: A payment of 45 leaves an account, and the balance afterwards is 128. Write an equation for the balance $s$ before the payment, and solve it.
blocks.solution:
The payment is subtracted from the starting balance: $s - 45 = 128$. The unknown is a starting number, so $s = 128 + 45 = 173$. Check: $173 - 45 = 128$.

The equation $128 + 45 = s$ describes the same situation, and by the theorem it is equivalent. A model fixes the relation between the quantities, not which of the equivalent equations is written down.

Find the value of the left side first.
items.solution: The left side is 7, so $\square - 4 = 7$ and $\square = 7 + 4 = 11$. Check: $11 - 4 = 7$.

items.q: A warehouse receives a delivery of 36 crates and then ships out 50, after which it holds 74 crates. Write one equation for the number $n$ of crates it held at the start, and solve it.
items.hint: Write the two events in order, then undo the last one first.
items.solution: $n + 36 - 50 = 74$. Undoing the shipment, $n + 36 = 74 + 50 = 124$; undoing the delivery, $n = 124 - 36 = 88$. Check: $88 + 36 = 124$ and $124 - 50 = 74$.

items.q: Find all whole-number solutions of $\square + \square = 10$, and all pairs of whole numbers that make $\square + \triangle = 10$ true. Why does the first equation have so few solutions?
items.hint: The same symbol stands for the same number each time it appears.
items.solution: In $\square + \square = 10$ both boxes hold one number, so its double is 10: the only solution is 5. In $\square + \triangle = 10$ the two symbols may differ, and the pairs are $(0, 10), (1, 9), \ldots, (10, 0)$: 11 pairs. Using one symbol twice is itself information, namely that the two numbers are equal, and that extra condition cuts 11 possibilities down to one.

blocks.title: The laws of equality
blocks.body: Equality is used in long arguments, not only in single checks. A few laws, all consequences of "same value", say what may be done with equations. In them $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ stand for any numbers, or any expressions.

blocks.title: Four laws of equality
blocks.body:
1. Reflexive: $a = a$.
2. Symmetric: if $a = b$, then $b = a$.
3. Transitive: if $a = b$ and $b = c$, then $a = c$.
4. Substitution: if $a = b$, then $a$ may be replaced by $b$ in any expression without changing its value, and in any equation without changing whether it is true.

Transitivity is what makes a chain $A = B = C = D$ useful: each link is checked on its own, and together they prove $A = D$.

$a = b$ says that $a$ and $b$ name one and the same number. Every number is itself, which is law 1. If $a$ and $b$ name the same number, so do $b$ and $a$, which is law 2. If $a$ and $b$ name one number and $b$ and $c$ name one number, all three name the same number, which is law 3. The value of an expression depends only on the values of its parts, not on how they are written, so replacing a part by another name for the same number changes nothing, which is law 4. For example, since $4 + 3 = 7$, we have $4 + 3 + 2 = 7 + 2 = 9$.

blocks.title: Doing the same to both sides
blocks.body:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be integers. If $a = b$, then

$$a + c = b + c \quad\text{and}\quad a - c = b - c.$$

Conversely, if $a + c = b + c$, or if $a - c = b - c$, then $a = b$. So adding the same number to both sides of an equation, or subtracting it, gives an equation with exactly the same solutions. For whole numbers all of this holds whenever the subtractions are possible, that is, when $c \le a$.

Start from $a + c = a + c$, true by law 1, and replace the second $a$ by $b$ (law 4): $a + c = b + c$. The same argument gives $a - c = b - c$.

For the converse, subtract $c$ from both sides of $a + c = b + c$. Since $(a + c) - c = a$ and $(b + c) - c = b$, the result is $a = b$. For subtraction, add $c$ to both sides of $a - c = b - c$: since $(a - c) + c = a$ and $(b - c) + c = b$, again $a = b$. So each step can be undone: a number makes the old equation true exactly when it makes the new one true.

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Circle
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.6, 3.6)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
def envelope(x, y):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), 1.0, 0.65, fc=(1.0, 0.92, 0.80), ec='orange', lw=1.5))
    ax.plot([x, x + 0.5, x + 1.0], [y + 0.65, y + 0.3, y + 0.65], color='orange', lw=1.2)
    ax.text(x + 0.5, y - 0.28, '$x$', ha='center', fontsize=14)
def counter(x, y, cross=False):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.2, fc='white', ec='black', lw=1.2))
    if cross:
        ax.plot([x - 0.21, x + 0.21], [y - 0.21, y + 0.21], color='red', lw=1.8)
        ax.plot([x - 0.21, x + 0.21], [y + 0.21, y - 0.21], color='red', lw=1.8)
def panel(y0, crossed):
    ax.plot([0, 7.4], [y0, y0], color='black', lw=0.8)
    ax.plot([3.4, 3.4], [y0, y0 + 1.5], color='black', lw=2.2)
    envelope(0.3, y0 + 0.45)
    for i in range(3):
        counter(1.8 + i * 0.55, y0 + 0.78, cross=crossed)
    for i in range(8):
        r, c = divmod(i, 4)
        counter(4.0 + c * 0.55, y0 + 1.05 - r * 0.55, cross=crossed and i >= 5)
panel(2.2, False)
ax.text(7.6, 2.95, '$x + 3 = 8$', fontsize=14, va='center')
panel(0.0, True)
ax.text(7.6, 0.75, '$x = 5$', fontsize=14, va='center')
ax.text(3.7, -0.35, 'take 3 counters from each side', ha='center', fontsize=11, color='red')
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 9.6); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 3.9); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')

blocks.body: Solve $x - 5 = 8$ and $14 = y + 9$.
blocks.solution:
Add 5 to both sides of the first: $x - 5 + 5 = 8 + 5$, so $x = 13$. Check: $13 - 5 = 8$.

Subtract 9 from both sides of the second: $14 - 9 = y + 9 - 9$, so $5 = y$. By the symmetric law this is $y = 5$; the unknown does not have to end on the left. Check: $5 + 9 = 14$.

Equations this short can also be read directly through the three-number theorem: $x - 5 = 8$ says $x = 8 + 5$. Doing the same to both sides matters because it keeps working when both sides carry operations: from $2x + 3 = x + 10$, subtracting $x$ and then 3 from both sides gives $x = 7$, and indeed $2 \times 7 + 3 = 17 = 7 + 10$.

blocks.title: Do the same to both sides, not to one
blocks.body: A frequent slip in solving $x + 3 = 8$ is to "move the 3 across" and write $x = 8 + 3 = 11$. Taking 3 off the left side and adding 3 to the right side is not doing the same to both sides: it lowers one side's value and raises the other's, so the new equation no longer says what the old one said. Substitution catches it at once: $11 + 3 = 14$, not 8. Subtracting 3 from both sides gives $x = 5$, and $5 + 3 = 8$.

items.q: If $b = a$ and $a = 9$, what is $b$, and which laws give it?
items.a: $b = 9$, by the transitive law (or by substituting 9 for $a$ in $b = a$).

items.hint: Undo the operation on $x$ by doing the opposite to both sides.

items.q: A student solves $x + 3 = 8$ by writing $x + 3 = 8 - 3 = 5$. The answer 5 is right. What is wrong with the working?
items.hint: Read the chain from its first expression to its last.
items.solution: By transitivity the chain claims $x + 3 = 5$, which is false when $x = 5$, and also $8 = 8 - 3$, which is false outright. Each line should be its own equation: $x + 3 = 8$, then $x = 8 - 3$, then $x = 5$.

items.q: Prove that if $a = b$ and $c = d$, then $a + c = b + d$.
items.hint: Start from $a + c = a + c$ and substitute twice.
items.solution: By law 1, $a + c = a + c$. Replace the $a$ on the right by $b$ (law 4, since $a = b$): $a + c = b + c$. Replace the $c$ on the right by $d$ (law 4, since $c = d$): $a + c = b + d$. Equal amounts added to equal amounts give equal totals.

items.q: Multiplying both sides of $x = 5$ by 0 gives $0 \times x = 0 \times 5$, which is true. Does the new equation have the same solutions as $x = 5$? What does this say about multiplying both sides by a number?
items.solution: No. $0 \times x = 0$ is true for every number $x$, for instance $0 \times 2 = 0$, so it has far more solutions than $x = 5$. Multiplying both sides by $c$ keeps a true equation true (substitution), but the step can be undone only by dividing by $c$, which is impossible when $c = 0$. So multiplying both sides by any number other than 0 keeps the solutions; multiplying by 0 loses all information.

items.q: A relation between whole numbers is called an equivalence relation if it obeys laws 1-3. Is "has the same last digit as" one? Is "differs by at most 1 from"? The chain $1 < 2 < 3$ is correctly used to conclude $1 < 3$: which of the laws does $<$ obey, and which one does the conclusion use?
items.solution: "Has the same last digit as" is: every number has its own last digit; if $m$ and $n$ share a last digit, so do $n$ and $m$; if $m$ shares it with $n$ and $n$ with $p$, all three share it. "Differs by at most 1 from" is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: 1 and 2 differ by 1, 2 and 3 differ by 1, but 1 and 3 differ by 2, so a chain of such steps proves nothing about its ends. The relation $<$ is transitive but neither reflexive ($1 < 1$ is false) nor symmetric ($1 < 2$ but not $2 < 1$), and the conclusion $1 < 3$ uses transitivity alone. Chains need transitivity, not the other two laws.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
Doing the same to both sides, extended to multiplying and dividing by numbers other than 0, solves every equation of the form $ax + b = c$ with $a \neq 0$, and several such equations in several unknowns are [[linear-systems]]. With $<$ in place of $=$ almost the same rules hold, with one exception: multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality ([[solving-inequalities]]). An equation that is true for every value of its letters, such as $a + b = b + a$, is an identity; rewriting expressions in algebra is a sequence of substitutions of equals, joined by transitivity.

The reflexive, symmetric and transitive laws define an equivalence relation ([[sets-relations]]). "Has the same remainder on division by $n$" is one, and it even respects substitution in sums and products; its arithmetic is [[congruences]]. In logic, equality is treated as part of the language, with the reflexive law and substitution as its rules of proof ([[logic-basics]]).

- An equation $A = B$ states that the expressions $A$ and $B$ have the same value; it is true or false, and either side may hold the calculation.
- Compensation: $(a + k) + (b - k) = a + b$ and $(a + k) - (b + k) = a - b$.
- An unknown stands for a number; a solution makes the equation true; substituting it back is a complete check.
- $a + b = c \iff c - a = b$, so one unknown among three numbers can be found in any position; the solution is unique, and may not exist among whole numbers.
- Equality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and equals may be substituted for equals; transitivity is why a chain of true equalities proves its ends equal.
- Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps exactly the same solutions.
